sections.body_md:
Singular value decomposition extends the stretch picture from symmetric matrices to every real matrix. Any \(A\) factors as \(U \Sigma V^T\). The orthogonal matrix \(V^T\) rotates the input into a special basis, the diagonal factor \(\Sigma\) stretches those axes by nonnegative singular values, and the orthogonal matrix \(U\) rotates the result into the output space.

The singular values are not the eigenvalues of a nonsymmetric \(A\). They are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the symmetric positive semidefinite matrix \(A^T A\). A negative eigenvalue of \(A\) itself contributes only its absolute value. The number of positive singular values is the rank. A zero singular value is a direction that \(A\) collapses, which is a nontrivial null vector of \(A\).

The reduced decomposition keeps only the positive singular values and the matching columns of \(U\) and \(V\). The full decomposition pads \(\Sigma\) out to the shape of \(A\) and keeps square orthogonal factors.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[
A = U \Sigma V^T, \qquad \sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(A^T A)}.
\]
The squares of the singular values sum to the squared Frobenius norm, which is also the sum of the squares of the entries. The largest singular value is the matrix 2-norm. The rank is the number of nonzero singular values. On a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix, the singular values and the eigenvalues agree.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(A^T A = \mathrm{diag}(0, 36)\). The eigenvalues are 0 and 36, so the singular values are 0 and 6. There is one nonzero singular value, and the rank is 1.

The largest singular value is the singular value 6. It is also the 2-norm and the Frobenius norm, because the other singular value does not contribute to the sum of squares. The columns are dependent: the first column is zero. A reduced decomposition keeps a single diagonal entry equal to 6 and drops the collapsed direction.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Do not read signed eigenvalues as singular values. A diagonal entry of \(-4\) produces the singular value 4. The spectral factorization \(U D U^T\) needs a symmetric matrix; a general matrix needs two different orthogonal factors. The product of the singular values is zero whenever the matrix is rank deficient, so that product is not the rank. Padding a reduced factorization back to a full one requires orthonormal columns in the padded directions, not zero columns.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The matrix 2-norm is the largest singular value, while the 1-norm and the infinity-norm have entrywise formulas as a maximum column sum and a maximum row sum. The Frobenius norm and the other Schatten norms are symmetric functions of the singular values. In linear least squares, a zero singular value means the columns are dependent and the minimizer is not unique.
